prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Do not use dashes, semicolons, colons or parentheses.

text:
On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. Apollo 13 was meant to be the third lunar landing, and by then the public had begun to treat such journeys as routine. Newspapers gave the launch little room. The commander, Jim Lovell, was a veteran of three earlier flights and was making his fourth trip into space. Fred Haise was the lunar module pilot and a rookie. The command module pilot was Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days before. The original pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and was grounded by flight surgeons, so Swigert took his seat after a frantic few days of training.

The spacecraft was really three machines joined together. The command module, which the crew named Odyssey, was a cone where the men would live and where they would later ride home. Behind it sat the service module, a cylinder packed with fuel, water and the oxygen and hydrogen tanks that fed the electrical power system. Tucked below was the lunar module, called Aquarius, a spindly craft built to carry two men to the surface and back. Their target was a rugged highland called Fra Mauro.

The first two days went smoothly. The crew carried out a television broadcast, and few people watched. Then, on the night of April 13, as Houston asked Swigert to stir the oxygen tanks, a routine job done to keep the supercold contents from stratifying, something went wrong. The craft was about 200,000 miles from Earth. A bang shook the cabin, warning lights flashed, and the ship lurched. Swigert said, "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell repeated it a moment later, and the phrase passed into history in its slightly altered form.

At first nobody understood how bad it was. Voltage was dropping. Oxygen pressure in one tank read zero, and the other was falling steadily. Lovell looked out a window and saw gas streaming into space, a sight that told him more than any instrument. The service module had been wrecked. Years later investigators would trace the cause to a chain of small errors. A thermostat switch in one oxygen tank had been damaged on the ground when technicians used higher voltage than it was built for during a test. When Swigert flipped the stirring fans, a spark from the bare wires ignited the Teflon insulation inside the tank, and the pressure burst through the tank and tore off a panel of the module.

Without oxygen, the fuel cells that made electricity and water would soon die. The command module would run on its small batteries, which were needed for the end of the trip. Mission control in Houston made a decision that was bold for its time. The Moon landing was abandoned, and the lunar module would become a lifeboat. Aquarius had been designed to support two men for roughly two days. Now it had to keep three alive for four. The crew climbed in, powered down Odyssey almost completely, and began a long, cold ordeal.

The next question was how to get home. The ship was on a path that would have taken it into lunar orbit, and returning from there would have required the damaged service module's main engine, which could not be trusted. Engineers considered turning around immediately, but that option needed the same engine and would have been a violent maneuver. Instead the flight directors chose to swing around the Moon and let its gravity bend the path back toward Earth. A free return trajectory is a natural loop of this kind, but Apollo 13 had left it earlier to aim at Fra Mauro, so a burn was needed to put the craft back on it. The crew fired Aquarius's descent engine, a motor never meant for this role, and corrected the course. Later, after rounding the far side of the Moon and reaching a distance of nearly 249,000 miles from Earth, the farthest any humans had traveled, they burned the engine again to speed up their return and aim for a Pacific splashdown a few hours sooner.

Life aboard was miserable. Aquarius was designed to be light, and it was not made for comfort. To save electricity the crew shut down nearly everything, including the heaters, and the cabin temperature fell toward freezing. Water condensed on the walls. Drinking water was rationed to a few ounces a day because the same supply was needed to cool the electronics, and the men grew dehydrated. Haise developed a fever and a painful infection. Nobody slept well in the cold. Lovell would lose about fourteen pounds over the flight.

A deadlier problem arrived through the air. Exhaled carbon dioxide was building up in the cabin, and the lithium hydroxide canisters in the lunar module that scrubbed it were running out. Plenty of spare canisters sat in Odyssey, but they were square and the lunar module's receptacles were round. The ground team gathered the items the astronauts had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a suit hose and duct tape, and then worked out an adapter step by step while the crew built it from a voice description. The contraption worked, and the gas levels dropped back to safe values. It stands as one of the great improvisations in the history of engineering.

Another challenge was waiting at the end. Odyssey had to be brought back to life after days dead in the cold, with only the limited battery power left. Ken Mattingly, the astronaut who had been bumped from the crew, spent long hours in a simulator in Houston working out a sequence that would power the systems on in the right order without draining the batteries. The team tested and rewrote it until it was safe, then read it to the crew.

As they approached Earth, a few small details also demanded manual work. The trajectory was drifting, and a correction burn was needed. With the main computer shut down to save power, Lovell lined the ship up by eye, using the edge of the sunlit Earth as a reference, and the crew timed a burn of about fourteen seconds by hand. On the final day they separated the damaged service module. As it drifted away, the crew photographed it and saw that an entire panel was missing and that the side was scorched and torn. It was the first time anyone had seen the full extent of the damage. Then they left Aquarius, which had served them so faithfully, and moved into Odyssey to prepare for the plunge.

On April 17 the capsule struck the atmosphere at roughly 25,000 miles per hour. A radio blackout is normal during this phase, lasting about three minutes, but this one dragged on, and the silence in Houston became unbearable. Controllers watched the clock pass the expected time and then pass it again. Finally, after nearly four minutes, Swigert's voice came through, and the room erupted. Three parachutes opened, and the capsule settled into the South Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. The crew had been gone nearly six days.

The mission was officially called a successful failure. The Moon landing never happened, but the three men came home alive, and the way a team on the ground and a crew in space solved problem after problem became a story that many people still draw from today. NASA redesigned the oxygen tanks and tightened its procedures before flying again. Apollo 14 went to Fra Mauro the following year. Lovell never walked on the Moon, but he had shown how a crew and thousands of people on Earth could face disaster together and win.
